title: Architecture as event space: Violence, securitisation, and resistance
geography: global, with focus on Israel/Palestine, US, UK, China
thesis: Architecture is an active political agent in security practices and resistance, analyzed through Tschumi's event space concept and Weizman's forensic architecture.
theme_1_justification: Tangential mention: discusses dual-use of architecture (e.g., hotel as Cold War project, Holiday Inn as militia base), but not focused on software/data dual-use. No engagement with information good properties.
theme_2_justification: Tangential: discusses forensic architecture as a practice to reveal hidden violence and contest official narratives (e.g., Hampton apartment, Weizman's work), but not centrally about algorithmic opacity or epistemic authority of data.
theme_3_justification: Substantive: conceptualizes buildings as 'event spaces' shaped by human action and violence; discusses security practices as modulating urban populations (checkpoints, walls, temporal rhythms); engages with smart city-like control (hotel geopolitics, MI6 building).
theme_4_justification: Substantive: discusses spatial destruction (Israeli occupation, wall, checkpoints, 'inverse geometry' of Nablus attack), home unmaking (Fred Hampton's apartment, Palestinian displacement), and forensic architecture as counter-forensics. Engages with Weizman's vertical sovereignty (drones) indirectly.
key_quotes: 'There is no architecture without action, no architecture without events, no architecture without program … no architecture without violence.' (Tschumi, quoted p. 368)
'buildings are not static entities … they continually undergo dynamic transformations' (Weizman, quoted p. 370)

'the architecture of occupation … [is met with] a counter architecture, which involves (among other things) redesigns that create possibilities of mobility that the Separation Wall and checkpoints stymie.' (p. 382)
policy_relevance: Implicitly calls for forensic architecture as a critical practice to document war crimes and human rights violations in urban contexts.
notes: Text is complete. Paper is theoretical, drawing on film, literature, and architectural theory. Dual-use is not a central concept; the focus is on architecture as a site of violence and resistance.
